title: Grace perfects nature (ST I.1.8)
hookLine: grace doesn't destroy nature but brings it to completion

cards: A piano tuner arrives at an old upright that hasn't been touched in years. She doesn't saw it in half or swap it for a synthesizer.
She opens the lid, finds the strings and hammers already there, and works on them one by one, until it sounds the way it was built to sound. Same wood. Same keys.
Only now, finished. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that works like that tuner. It's tucked into a reply early in the Summa, and it shapes how he holds faith and reason, God and the ordinary person.

teach.b: It comes in the Summa's very first question, at the eighth article: does sacred teaching argue? Yes, Thomas says.

Not to prove the faith, which rests on what God has revealed, but to start from it and make other things clear. Then an objection: if faith rests on God's word, doesn't bringing in human reason cheapen it?
His reply, put plainly: grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it. So natural reason should serve faith, the way the will's natural leaning serves love. Nature is what a thing is made with.
For a person: a mind that asks why, a body, a temperament, hands that can learn a craft. Grace is God's free gift. Thomas sets two pictures aside.

teach.h: NOT A BULLDOZER, NOT A STICKER.
teach.b: In one, grace is a bulldozer: to be holy, stop being human. Flatten the mind, scorn the body. In the other, grace is a sticker, pasted on top, leaving you just as you were.
Thomas's picture is the tuner: grace works on what's already there and brings it to completion. He shows it in the same reply.
Paul, preaching in Athens, quotes the Greeks' own poets.

teach.h: FOR WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims, Acts gives his words: "as some also of your own poets said: For we are also his offspring." A pagan poet's line, put to work for the gospel. Reason wasn't thrown out.

It was given a job. So Catholic teaching can say your curiosity, your humor, your patience with a tangled knot are not rivals to holiness. Catholics say grace takes them further than they could go alone.

how: Catholic teachers often use Thomas's line that grace perfects nature to explain why the Church values reason, science, art and ordinary human gifts alongside faith.

o: nature is good, so grace isn't really needed
God's gift works only on people born gifted
God's gift completes what we are, not erases it

games.q: grace perfects nature — tap the pairs.
p: what a thing is, what it's made with
to be holy, stop being human

s: Thomas says grace replaces human nature with something new
he says grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it.
the line comes in a reply to an objection, early in the Summa
the first question, eighth article, answering whether reason cheapens faith.
Thomas says sacred teaching argues in order to prove the faith
he says it argues from the faith, to make other things clear; reason serves faith.

games.q: an objector says to Thomas: if faith rests on God's word, bringing in human reason only cheapens it. what does Thomas answer?
o: he agrees, and leaves reason out.
reason serves faith, because grace doesn't destroy nature but perfects it.
reason is the judge, and faith must pass its test.
games.why: Thomas says natural reason should serve faith, the way the will's natural leaning serves love, and points to Paul quoting a Greek poet in Athens.

practice: Name one thing you were simply made with: a quick mind, steady hands, a good ear, a knack for putting people at ease, then a second and a third if they come. Notice you didn't earn them.
If you pray, thank God for each one by name; if you don't, hold them a moment as things given.

wordCard.voice: Grace perfects nature. Thomas Aquinas's line from the Summa's first question: God's gift doesn't wipe out what we are, it brings it to completion.

orig.s: gratia non tollat naturam, sed perficiat
orig.say: GRAH-tsee-ah non TOL-laht nah-TOO-rahm, sed per-FEE-chee-aht
orig.note: Latin, from Summa I.1.8: grace does not take away nature, but perfects it.

carryVoice: Your line: grace completes. Not a bulldozer, and not a sticker either. See you tomorrow.
